[[File:Lamium album 2 BOGA.jpg|thumb|Close-up of flowers]]
'''''Lamium album''''', commonly called '''white dead-nettle''',<ref name=BSBI_Atlas2020>{{cite web |title=White Dead-nettle ''Lamium album'' L. |work=BSBI Online Plant Atlas 2020 |editor1=P.A. Stroh |editor2=T. A. Humphrey |editor3=R.J. Burkmar |editor4=O.L. Pescott |editor5=D.B. Roy |editor6=K.J. Walker |publisher=Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland |date=2020 |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.8rg |access-date=20 July 2024 }}</ref><ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007|accessdate=2024-07-20}}</ref> is a [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Lamiaceae]]. It is native throughout [[Europe]] and [[Asia]], growing in a variety of habitats from open [[grassland]] to woodland, generally on moist, fertile [[soil]]s.

==Description==
[[File:Bombus hortorum - Laminum album.jpg|thumb|right|Yellow-haired male ''[[Bombus lucorum]]'' feeding from ''Lamium album'']]
''Lamium album'' is a [[rhizomatous]] herbaceous [[perennial]] plant growing to {{convert|70|cm|abbr=on}} tall,<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Francis-Baker |first=Tiffany |title=Concise Foraging Guide |date=2021 |publisher=[[Bloomsbury Publishing|Bloomsbury]] |isbn=978-1-4729-8474-6 |series=[[The Wildlife Trusts]] |location=London |pages=48}}</ref> with green, four-angled stems. The [[leaves]] are {{convert|3-8|cm|abbr=on|frac=2}} long and {{convert|2-5|cm|abbr=on|frac=8}} broad, triangular with a rounded base, softly hairy, and with a serrated margin and a petiole up to {{convert|5|cm|abbr=on|frac=8}} long; like many other members of the Lamiaceae, they appear superficially similar to those of the stinging nettle ''[[Urtica dioica]]'' but do not sting,<ref name=":0" /> hence the common name "dead-nettle". The [[flower]]s are white, produced in whorls ('verticillasters') on the upper part of the stem, the individual flowers {{convert|1.5-2.5|cm|abbr=on|frac=8}} long.

===Phytochemistry===
Various [[polyphenol|polyphenolic glycosides]] such as Lamalboside and [[Verbascoside]], Tiliroside and [[5-caffeoylquinic acid]] along with [[Rutoside]] and [[quercetin 3-O-glucoside]] and [[kaempferol 3-O-glucoside]] can be isolated from the flowers of ''L. album''.<ref>Phenylpropanoid esters from Lamium album flowers. Jaromir Budzianowski and Lutoslawa Skrzypczak, Phytochemistry, March 1995, Volume 38, Issue 4, Pages 997–1001, {{doi|10.1016/0031-9422(94)00727-B}}</ref> The plant also contains the [[iridoid]] glycosides [[lamalbid]], [[alboside A]] and [[alboside B|B]], and [[caryoptoside]]<ref>Iridoid glucosides from Lamium album. Søren Damtoft, Phytochemistry, January 1992, Volume 31, Issue 1, Pages 175–178, {{doi|10.1016/0031-9422(91)83030-O}}</ref> as well as the hemiterpene glucoside [[hemialboside]].<ref>Hemialboside, a hemiterpene glucoside from Lamium album. Søren Damtoft and Søren Rosendal Jensen, Phytochemistry, July 1995, Volume 39, Issue 4, Pages 923–924, {{doi|10.1016/0031-9422(95)00085-L}}</ref>

''L.album'' was a source of chlorophyll and other plant pigments for [[Mikhail Tsvet]], the inventor of adsorption chromatography.<ref>Source book in chemistry 1900-1950, edited by Henry Leicester, p.23.</ref>

==Taxonomy==
''Lamium album'' was described and named by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1753.{{r|IPNI:448792-1}}

==Distribution and habitat==
''L. album''  is native to Eurasia, from Ireland in the west to Japan in the east. It has three subspecies, subsp. ''album'' in the western part of the range, subsp. ''crinitum'' in the southern part in southwest Asia (Turkey to Nepal), and subsp. ''barbatum'' in the far east of mainland Asia and in Japan.<ref name="POWO">{{Cite POWO |last1=POWO |author-link1=Plants of the World Online |id=448792-1 |title=''Lamium album'' L. |access-date=20 July 2024 }}</ref><ref name=DVF>{{cite web| title=Den Virtuella Floran: ''Lamium album'' L.|url=http://linnaeus.nrm.se/flora/di/lamia/lamiu/lamialbv.jpg |first=A. |last=Anderberg |publisher=Museum of Natural History, Stockholm |access-date=19 May 2016}}</ref> It is common in England, rare in the west and northern Scotland, and introduced to eastern Ireland.<ref>Clapham, A.R., Tutin, T.G. and Warburg, E.F. ''Excursion Flora of the British Isles.'' Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|0-521-04656-4}}</ref> It is abundant in the British Isles, where it is found on roadsides, around hedges, and in abandoned places.<ref name=BSBI_Atlas2020/><ref>Parnell, J. and Curtis, T. 2012. ''Webb's An Irish Flora''. p.360 Cork University Press. {{ISBN|978-185918-4783}}</ref><ref>Hackney, P. (Ed) 1992. ''Stewart and Corry's Flora of the North-east of Ireland.'' Institute of Irish Studies and The Queen's University of Belfast. {{ISBN|0-85389-446-9}}</ref>

''L. album'' was introduced to [[North America]], where it is widely [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]].

==Ecology==
The flowers are visited by many types of insects, but mostly by long-tongued insects, like bees.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Van Der Kooi |first1=C. J. |last2=Pen |first2=I. |last3=Staal |first3=M. |last4=Stavenga |first4=D. G. |last5=Elzenga |first5=J. T. M. |year=2015 |title=Competition for pollinators and intra-communal spectral dissimilarity of flowers |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/273158762 |journal=Plant Biology |volume=18 |issue=1 |pages=56–62 |doi=10.1111/plb.12328 |pmid=25754608|hdl=11370/caee8d0d-9724-4056-9d45-93162a5a7afc |hdl-access=free }}</ref> [[Bumblebee]]s are especially attracted to the flowers, which are a good source of early nectar and pollen, hence the plant is sometimes called the '''bee nettle'''.<ref>[http://www.botanical.com/botanical/mgmh/n/nettle03.html botanical.com - A Modern Herbal | Nettles<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.wildlifetrusts.org/wildlife-explorer/wildflowers/white-dead-nettle|title=White dead-nettle | the Wildlife Trusts}}</ref> 

==Uses==
The young shoots and leaves can be cooked as a vegetable.<ref name=":0" />

==Cultural significance==
A distillation of the flowers is reputed "to make the heart merry, to make a good colour in the face, and to make the vital spirits more fresh and lively."<ref>{{cite book|url=http://www.botanical.com/botanical/mgmh/n/nettle03.html#whi|publisher=Botanical.com|chapter=NETTLE, WHITE DEAD|author=Mrs M. Grieve|title=A Modern Herbal|year=1931}}</ref>
